newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr gives impression of a fixed currency.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr gives impression of a fixed currency.

text.p: The Australian dollar offered every impression of being a fixed currency Thursday, making no effort to escape the cramped US$0.7480/7530 range held all week.
There was some thought of support related to a A$1.0 billion global eurobond launched for Fannie Mae Wednesday, but dealers suspected much of the A$ buying for this had already been done.

Some brave souls were touting the case against another RBA rate cut and doubts were even creeping into the futures pit. But most had been too badly burned by the surprise cut in May to risk going long yet. The approach of the quarter and financial year-end provided another excuse, if needed, for inactivity.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar was still at US$0.7509/14 from an early US$0.7505/10 and US$0.7509/14 late here Wednesday.
On the crosses it recouped a little of Wednesday's one yen loss to stand at 85.45/55 yen from 85.20/30 and edged up to 57.0 in trade weighted terms from 56.9.
It has languished in a US$0.7470/7540 range since June 11 when it was evicted from atop 76 cents in the wake of data showing a shock 40,300 fall in May employment.
Those had the money market baying for a rate cut and saw the September bank bill contract surge to a 94.94 high, implying a rate of 5.06 percent against the present 5.50 percent cash rate.
But two weeks without a major release had seen memories fade, and the bill contract with them to 94.75 today.
Arguments against another official cut were back in vogue -- and were much the same as those heard before the last easing on May 23 although events afterward more than justified the move.

The weak jobs data could be explained away as a lagging indicator and, anyway, unemployment was kept high by structural problems in the Australian labour market which monetary policy alone could not solve, analysts said.
In contrast, forward indicators like housing and job ads pointed to a pickup in economic growth later in the year.

The full impact of past easings was yet to be felt, the argument went, while the offshore scene was also supportive of growth here with the U.S. running above trend and evidence at long last of a real recovery in Japan and Europe.
Furthermore, the depreciation in the A$ since the last rate cut -- about three percent in trade weighted terms -- was a de facto easing in monetary conditions of itself.

And there was the risk of a tightening in the U.S. in the next few months which would further widen the US$'s yield advantage and possibly put the local currency under more pressure, which in turn could threaten imported inflation.
Most analysts, while conceding some of these points, still reckon the chance of a cut in July or August is 50/50 or better.

"The case for a further easing is finely balanced - signs of a pick up in activity are slowly coming through but it is happening in an unconvincing fashion," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
"Capacity constraints and hence inflation pressures are still a long way off," he added.
That was a crucial point since, if the economy could run a lot faster without risking price pressures, it was not the job of the central bank to stand in its way.
With inflation set to slow further it was argued an easing was needed just to keep real rates from rising, said analysts.
A Reuter survey of economists last week found they expected the consumer price index to reach a median low of 0.7 percent and underlying inflation to hit 1.7 percent.
The latter implied a real interest rate of 380 basis points, which was not far from the 420 basis point seen in Q1 1996 when inflation peaked at 3.3 percent and rates at 7.50 percent.
"What's the point of suffering to get low inflation if you can't have the pleasure of low interest rates?" was a rehtorical question often posed. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
